anchors.fact: The Seelbach was created in 1995 by Adam Seger at the Seelbach Hotel in Louisville, who presented it as the hotel's rediscovered pre-Prohibition signature drink (sources give 1912 or ca. 1917 for the invented date — never state a year).
anchors.meaning: A trick good enough to fool the experts: received wisdom challenged.
anchors.speaksTo: drawnToward: Mischief · soughtFor: A little chaos

anchors.fact: The invented origin was an accident: a bartender spilling champagne into a Manhattan.
anchors.meaning: The Trickster's craft is making the planned look accidental; fear of unintended results turned inside out.

anchors.fact: Newspapers and respected cocktail books repeated the story for about twenty years, until Seger confessed in 2016. The drink is still served at the hotel and discussed as a modern classic.
anchors.meaning: The trick changed nothing about the drink, and exposed how much we trust what's called "old". A mark left.
anchors.speaksTo: drawnToward: Change · soughtFor: A reality check, Ideas

anchors.fact: Built in the glass and never stirred, over a bitters-soaked sugar cube that dissolves slowly.
anchors.meaning: The drink changes as it goes; the last sips differ from the first. The truth is at the bottom.

anchors.fact: Seger said he was "nobody" in the bar world at the time and wanted the drink as a promotion for the hotel (quoted from his 2016 confession).
anchors.meaning: Our reading, not fact: a trick with a gift inside. He gave people a great drink, a great story to enjoy it with, and eventually the truth. Disruption with a point, a mark left.

anchors.fact: The sugar cube soaked in bitters comes from the classic Champagne Cocktail, an Old-Fashioned with champagne in place of whiskey.
anchors.meaning: An old trick in new hands.

cocktail.closingLine: Don't stir it. It tells you the truth at the end.
method: Soak the sugar cube with both bitters and drop it into the flute.
Add the bourbon and the orange liqueur.
Top slowly with the champagne. Do not stir.
Squeeze the orange peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.
cocktail.name: No Accident
cocktail.tagline: You never break a rule by accident.

reading.epigraph: The story was a trick. The drink never was.
whoYouAre: You see the strings. Where other people see how things are, you see how they were decided, and who decided them, and you can't resist giving those strings a tug.

You say your truest things as jokes, because a joke slips past people's guard where an argument never would. What looks like chaos from the outside is, in your head, a plan three moves ahead. You would rather be misunderstood than boring, and you'd rather shake a room than disappear in it. Here's what most people miss about you: underneath the mischief, you care a great deal. Every trick is really an invitation to see what you see. What scares you isn't getting caught. It's being ignored.
yours: In 1995, a bartender at an old hotel in Louisville, Kentucky, introduced a cocktail he said he'd found in the hotel's past: its signature drink from before Prohibition, born when a bartender spilled champagne into a Manhattan by accident. It was a perfect story. Newspapers repeated it. Respected cocktail books printed it. For twenty years, people who knew a great deal about drinks raised their glasses to a piece of history.

There was no history. In 2016 he admitted he had invented the drink himself, and the story with it. No accident, no century-old recipe. And here's the part you'll like: nothing about the drink changed. It tasted just as good the day after the confession as the day before, and it's still poured at that hotel.

So why do it? He later said that back then he was a nobody, with no name in the bar world, and he wanted to put the hotel on the map. That's the reason he gave. But I like to think there was more to it. He knew a good drink with no past is easy to walk past, and a drink with a legend gets ordered, loved and passed on. So he played a trick with a gift inside: he gave people a great drink, a great story to enjoy it with, and in the end the truth as well. It showed how powerful a good story is, and how quickly people will rally behind one. All it takes is a little magic to set it going.

That's your kind of magic: never a trick for its own sake. So this is his drink, played your way. Bourbon, orange liqueur and two kinds of bitters, poured over a sugar cube and topped with champagne, and never stirred. It changes as it goes. The top is bright and dry. The sugar at the bottom dissolves slowly, sending up a thin line of bubbles, so the last sips are sweeter, darker and more bitter than the first. The truth is at the bottom of the glass, which is exactly where you would hide it. And the story it was first sold with was about an accident. You know better: the best tricks only look like accidents.

Here's what I'd ask of you. The next time you feel like pulling the rug out from under a room, make it a trick with a gift inside, and leave people with something better than what they walked in with. Then stay long enough to show them how it was done. The trick is what they'll remember tonight. The gift is what they'll keep.
